job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Welcome, Amira, and thank you. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me the public version and the private one. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in software systems at Eastvale, and I live with my parents above our family grocery shop. I'm up for early prayer, then I help my mother stock shelves before I take the tram to campus. In the evening I do the shop's accounts on a spreadsheet I built, then I call my fiancé, Idris, who works two towns over.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Software engineering, passed with an average mark. I was working at the shop on weekends and holidays, so I never had time for an internship, which I regret. My final project was an ordering app for the shop's suppliers, and my father now uses it more than I expected, which makes me proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for most people, because it means things stay steady. I use a chatbot now and then to explain code errors and it helps a bit, but I wouldn't hand it the shop's money. I'd tell my aunties and friends that there's no need to be afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be under pressure, just a different kind. I owe about 10,000 and want to marry Idris within two years. The wedding costs and a flat deposit are my real concern, and I need a proper job to start any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and apply to software companies in Eastvale and two banks, and I'd keep running the shop's accounts so I earn a little. I'd talk to Idris about a modest wedding, not the big one my aunties imagine. And I'd keep saving the 150 a month I put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful but pressed. Like carrying a heavy bag in a warm room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a modest wedding mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sixty guests instead of two hundred, a hall at the community centre, and food from our own shop. My mother cried a little when I said it, then said it sounds sensible. I'd choose a small wedding with no debt over a big one that I'd still be paying off in my thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the job search feel different because of the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I can't just wait for the perfect role. I'd take a decent one even if it's not exciting. Idris earns steadily, but we want to start our home on solid ground, not on guesses.

say: AI is **handy** for explaining code errors, but there's no need to be afraid.
Things stay **steady**, which is good news for most people.
think: The pressure is my **10,000 loan** and wanting to marry within two years.
I need a proper **job** to start the wedding and flat.
do: **Apply** to Eastvale software firms and two banks.
**Keep** doing the shop's accounts for a small income.
**Plan** a modest wedding and save 150 a month.
feel: **Hopeful** but pressed, like a heavy bag in a warm room.
S0.quote: I'd choose a small wedding with no debt over a big one that I'd still be paying off in my thirties.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **family and wedding** costs, not AI.
Chooses a **modest wedding** to avoid debt, matching her values.
Accepts a decent job over a perfect one because of her **timeline**.

steps.text: Apply to Eastvale software firms and two banks
Keep doing the shop's accounts for small pay
Save 150 a month toward the wedding and flat deposit
Plan a modest wedding with sixty guests at the community centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will be hard for some and good for others, and we should look after those who struggle. I'd tell people in my community to learn what the tools do and not to fear them. We've always adapted, haven't we?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried. Junior programming is exactly what these tools do, and I've no work experience. Idris is a delivery planner, a desk job, and I've read that planning is among the first things to go. If both of us are hit, we'd be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tools properly, every day, on my projects. I'd look for jobs that need people who understand a business, not just code, like software for shops and suppliers. I'd also ask my father's wholesale suppliers if they need an app built or maintained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I try to stay practical. Being busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both of you could be hit. What would that look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris's firm already had a hiring freeze, he told me last week. If his job went and mine didn't come, we'd delay the wedding and live above the shop longer. My fiancé and I would be two people with degrees, one loan and nobody hiring, which is not how we pictured starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your faith come into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me calm, and it also gives me people. If things went wrong, the community would help, and I'd help others. Last winter we collected for a family who lost work. That's how it works where we live.

Our community should learn what the tools do, not **fear** them.
think: Junior programming is **exactly** what these tools do.
Idris is a delivery planner, and **both** of us could be hit.
do: **Use** the tools every day on my projects.
**Look** for jobs in software for shops and suppliers.
Ask my father's **suppliers** if they need an app maintained.
S1.quote: My fiancé and I would be two people with degrees, one loan and nobody hiring, which is not how we pictured starting out.
fieldNote: The risk is **household-wide** because her fiancé's desk job is exposed too.
Her **community** is both comfort and a practical safety net.
Steady learner: adopts the tools once she sees they are **proven**.

steps.text: Use an AI coding tool daily on the supplier app
Apply for software jobs at shops and distributors
Ask the community and family for introductions to employers
Hold the wedding date flexible until both jobs are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we must stand together as families. Two years is nothing, and the government can't wave it away. I'd say that our community should keep a fund, as we've always done for emergencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be afraid. The planning job that Idris does and the software job that I'm training for would both go. We'd have nothing coming in except the shop, and the shop isn't big enough for four of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding, or make it a tiny ceremony at home. I'd work in the shop full time and use my software skills to make it more efficient, ordering and stock. I'd put every pound against the loan, and I'd ask the community fund if things get bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold fear. I'd pray a lot, and I'd cry once and then get to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Idris?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gently, and over tea. I'd say we'll do this together, whatever happens, and that the wedding date matters less than the marriage. I'd tell my fiancé Idris I'd marry him in the shop's back room with sixty tins of beans as decoration if it came to that. He'd laugh. Then we'd count the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shop need to survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A better supply deal and fewer wasted goods. My ordering app helps with that, and I'd make it stronger. In that world people still buy food, so a shop should hold on. It isn't the career I trained for, but it's real.

say: We must **stand together** as families; the government can't wave it away.
Our community should keep a **fund** for emergencies.
think: Both Idris's planning job and my **software job** would go.
The shop couldn't support **four** of us, so we would be in real trouble.
do: **Postpone** the wedding or make it a tiny ceremony.
**Work** full time in the shop and improve ordering with my app.
Put every pound against the **loan** and ask the community fund if needed.
feel: **Cold fear**, a prayer, one cry, then work.
S2.quote: I'd tell my fiancé Idris I'd marry him in the shop's back room with sixty tins of beans as decoration if it came to that.
fieldNote: Household exposure is the **centre**: two exposed earners and one small shop.
Turns to **faith and community** instead of protest.
Humour with **Idris** shows how she copes.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding or hold a small ceremony at home
Work full time in the shop and use the ordering app to cut waste
Put every spare pound against the loan
Ask the community fund for help if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something we can plan around. I'd tell my cousins to marry, save and learn a skill, in that order, and to keep family close. I'd also say we should push local councils to run retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more hopeful. I'd have a first job and two or three years of experience, and Idris and I might have married and bought a small flat. Even if it all changes, we'd have a base.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first sensible software job and marry within two years, modestly. We'd put 400 a month into a flat deposit between us. I'd learn the tools well enough to be the one at work who checks them. And I'd keep the shop's accounts so my father has help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. It's a heavy thought, but I can see us having a home by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'a base' mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat that's paid for or almost, and an emergency fund, and family nearby. That way, if the work goes, we aren't starting from nothing. A home we own and a family who lives around the corner is my idea of security, more than any job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Timing. If AGI comes sooner than the card, we'd have bought a flat just as work disappears. I'd hold back on the biggest purchase until we're sure, perhaps rent a bit longer than my aunties would like.

say: Five years is something we can **plan** around, and our families can prepare.
Marry, save and learn a skill, in that **order**.
think: I'd have a first job, and maybe a **small flat** with Idris.
A home and family nearby is **security** if work goes.
do: **Take** the first sensible software job and marry modestly in two years.
**Put** 400 a month with Idris into a flat deposit.
Learn the tools well enough to **check** them at work.
feel: **Better**: heavy, but I can see us having a home.
S3.quote: A home we own and a family who lives around the corner is my idea of security, more than any job title.
fieldNote: Time lets her plan a **life**: wedding, flat and a job.
Values **home and family** over job titles.
Still anxious because the **timing** could go wrong.

steps.text: Take the first sensible software job offered
Hold a modest wedding within two years
Save 400 a month with Idris for a flat deposit
Learn AI tools well enough to check their output at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and we should use it for our children and not just ourselves. I'd tell people to build skills, save, and strengthen their communities, because that's what carries you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be at ease. By 34 I could have a good job, a home, and two children, God willing. Robots for hands-on work come late, and by then my career is well along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in software for a few years, marry, and buy a flat. I'd save for the children's schooling. And I'd study the new tools each year, so I'm the person at work who's already learnt them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. There's room in it for a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by using it for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want mine to grow up with a parent who's calm about this, not panicked. If my children ask me what to study, I want to say something true, and I'd like ten years to find out what that is. I don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that bothers you about ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people might relax too much, and then get caught. I'd keep a yearly family meeting about money and plans, like my father does about the shop. It sounds dull but it keeps us honest.

say: Ten years is a **blessing**; use it for our children too.
Build skills, save, and strengthen our **communities**, because that is what carries you.
think: By 34 I could have a good job, a **home** and two children.
Robots reach hands-on work **late**, when my career is well along.
do: **Work** in software for a few years, then marry and buy a flat.
feel: **Peaceful**, mostly, with room in it for a family.
S4.quote: If my children ask me what to study, I want to say something true, and I'd like ten years to find out what that is.
fieldNote: A decade turns her worry into **parenting** plans.
Wants honest **advice** for her future children.
Keeps a **yearly family meeting** about money, copied from her father.

steps.text: Work in software for several years and move up
Marry, buy a flat and plan for children
Save a schooling fund for the children
Study one new AI tool each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both Idris and I have exposed jobs and no time to rebuild. What would help is a community fund backed by government, retraining that pays a wage, and clear guidance for young couples.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not only worried for myself. Behind every graduate there's a family with a shop or a salary, and a bad year for us is a bad year for all of them.

headlineQuote: Behind every graduate there's a family with a shop or a salary, and a bad year for us is a bad year for all of them.
portrait: Amira is 24, doing a **software systems** master's after a pass in software engineering.
She lives above her family's **grocery shop** in Eastvale and keeps its accounts.
Traditional and steady, she uses AI **now and then** and leans on faith and community.
She is engaged to **Idris**, a delivery planner whose desk job is exposed too.
Her mood runs from uneasy to alarmed, and the **household** and wedding costs sit at the centre.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, since both she and her fiancé could lose work.
whatWouldHelp: A **community fund** backed by government, wage-paying retraining and guidance for young couples.
